meta.title: Reinforcement Learning-Optimized Sensor Placement for Boosting Large-Scale Surrogate Hydrological Models
meta.authorsHtml: Amir Aieb<sup>∗</sup><sup>1</sup>, Miguel Pincheira<sup>1</sup>, Massimo Vecchio<sup>1</sup>, Fabio Antonelli<sup>1</sup>

abstract: Reliable estimation of potential evapotranspiration (PET) over large spatial domains is challenged by sparse observations, heterogeneous terrain, and the computational cost of physically based models. This work introduces a technique for selecting representative sensor locations and training a 3DCNN surrogate model for accurate large-scale gridded PET prediction. To address the sensor-placement challenge, we reframe sensor data as a pixel-selection problem within the reinforcement-learning (RL) workflow. Using SRTM elevation and CHELSA temperature inputs across Italian catchments, the RL-based approach improves spatial alignment in XGBoost-selected pixels by over 70%. Moreover, it optimises and preserves the data pattern using only 2% of the full pixels. The resulting technique enhances predictive performance of surrogate model compared to the baseline methods and supports scalable, spatially coherent PET estimation under data-sparse conditions.

blocks.html: Data scarcity and the uneven distribution of in-situ sensors remain major challenges in environmental monitoring, particularly for hydrological variables such as potential evapotranspiration (PET) [1]. Sparse monitoring networks limit the reliable characterisation of spatiotemporal variability and reduce the capacity to validate satellite-derived products, increasing reliance on modelling approaches to fill observational gaps [2, 3]. Physically based PET models are widely used for this purpose, yet they were originally developed for point-scale applications, and extending them across large spatial grids and long temporal periods introduces a substantial computational burden as spatial resolution and temporal frequency increase [4, 5].

Data-driven PET modelling faces major scalability challenges because environmental datasets are highdimensional, heterogeneous, and governed by nonlinear relationships that vary across space and time [6]. Surrogate modelling offers an efficient alternative, but its performance depends on the underlying architecture. Long Short- Term Memory (LSTM) networks struggle with transfer learning because their internal states are tied to the structure and ordering of the training data [7, 8]. Convolution-based models such as 3DCNNs, ConvLSTMs, and hybrid CNN-LSTM extract spatial and spatio-temporal patterns more effectively, yet their reliance on fixed input shapes and regular grids limits generalisation across basins with different geometries or resolutions [9–11]. Transformer-based models handle variable-sized inputs more flexibly, but their high memory and computational demands make large-scale, high-resolution PET prediction impractical without substantial HPC resources. These constraints make scalable and transferable PET surrogate models difficult to achieve [12].

To address these limitations, we develop a reinforcement learning (RL)–driven surrogate framework that identifies and optimises monitoring site locations. A multi-objective function selects the most informative sites and reduces the initial sensor set generated by the XGBoost classifier. Within the RL workflow, an integrated genetic-algorithm permutation relocates misaligned sensors by swapping their positions with other valid candidates in the same region, evaluating each rearrangement based on how well it preserves the underlying percentile structure of the full field. A surrogate deep-learning model is then trained on the refined sparse observations and evaluated across the full gridded domain. In this formulation, each sensor location corresponds to a pixel on the spatial grid, allowing placement to be specified directly within the spatial field. The gridded setup provides a controlled environment to assess the RL workflow and evaluate how different sensor configurations affect field reconstruction. This grid-based design is broadly applicable beyond PET, supporting any task that requires spatially coherent ground-truth acquisition through strategically positioned sensors.

The paper is organised as follows. Section 2 introduces the study area, data, and methodology; Section 3 presents the results and discussion; and Section 4 concludes with final remarks and future work.

The study area covers nearly 189,000 km<sup>2</sup> across northern and central Italy and includes eight hydrological basins ranging from high-elevation Alpine headwaters to lowlying plains and coastal regions (Figure 1).

The dataset includes SRTM elevation values at 1 km resolution, ranging from about 3 to 3,568 m, capturing strong topographic variability across the basins and supporting the optimisation of sensor placement [13]. Daily CHELSA temperatures (2020–2022) follow the expected seasonal cycle and were used to build the surrogate hydrological model for large-scale PET prediction [14]. Daily PET from the PM-FAO dataset (2020–2022) shows the opposite seasonal pattern [15], remaining low in winter and rising in summer, and served as dataset benchmark [15] (see Figure 2).

This section introduces an RL-based surrogate modelling framework that aims to select a small set of representative in-situ locations, treated as individual pixels, to train the hydrological model using the most informative and physically meaningful data. Applied to PET estimation using CHELSA temperature data, it addresses strong spatial heterogeneity in complex terrain and the challenge of model calibration under sparse data, enabling more robust model development across multi-scale spatial domains. The specific components of the framework are described in the subsequent steps following Figure 3.

Step 1 identifies candidate pixel locations (CPL) that capture the geophysical variability of the study region under limited data availability. In this study, XGBoost is applied to classify the DEM considering its geophysical coordinates as input, enabling a more accurate extraction of representative terrain classes within the masked region [16]. The choice of geophysical parameters remains flexible and can be adapted to the hydrological processes and landscape characteristics of interest.

Step 2 introduces an RL agent that (i) minimises the number of selected pixels, (ii) detects pixels whose distributions deviate from the full dataset, and (iii) repositions these misaligned pixels through GA-based shuffling. A reward function balances pixel-count reduction with preserving similarity to regional geophysical characteristics, and the agent is trained using Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO), a policy-gradient method that stabilises learning by constraining policy updates and preventing overly large parameter shifts [17]. Starting from the XGBoost-derived subset, the agent runs an iterative verification loop in which each candidate subset is evaluated using the Kolmogorov– Smirnov (KS) statistic, the squared Wasserstein distance (W<sup>2</sup>), and the Mean Percentile Difference (MPD) [18–20]. These metrics shape the reward, enabling the agent to remove redundant pixels while maintaining distributional fidelity and converge on the minimal subset that still reflects the statistical properties of the full dataset.

Pixels hat fail to capture the regional elevation density are classified as misaligned or underrepresented. The RL agent detects these by computing each pixel’s MPD relative to the regional elevation distribution and analysing the spread of MPD values. Thresholds of ±10m for minor deviations and ±50m for major deviations are derived from the empirical distribution of elevation differences [21]. Using thresholds grounded in observed elevation variability enables systematic detection of pixels that diverge from regional density patterns and ensures they are flagged for repositioning during the action phase.

A GA is used as the RL agent’s action mechanism, operating within masked DEM regions where misaligned pixels occur and adjusting their locations through permutations with other valid candidates from the same region. Each individual encodes a subset of pixel locations from the masked area, and fitness is evaluated by how closely the subset reproduces the full dataset’s percentile distribution using MPD. The GA applies two-point crossover, shuffle mutation, and tournament selection, running with a population of 100 over 200 generations [19]. Integrated into the RL framework, this action step enables the agent to produce a corrected pixel set that remains consistent with the global distribution.

Step 3 uses the refined representative pixel locations to extract climate values from satellite-derived fields or other sensor datasets, creating a realistic scenario in which the surrogate model receives inputs at the same spatial resolution used later for large-scale prediction. These extracted values show how in-situ measurements collected at the selected sensor positions would feed into model training and propagate through the surrogate-modelling workflow.

Step 4 establishes the hydrological response variable used to train the surrogate model. Daily PET is computed using the Hamon method applied to the extracted CHELSA temperature pixels data, a widely adopted and well-validated approach in hydrological modelling [22]. These PET estimates form the surrogate model’s response variable, and in operational settings the same variable could be obtained directly from in-situ sensors installed at the optimised monitoring locations, keeping the workflow fully compatible with real-world measurement networks.

Step 5 introduces the 3DCNN surrogate model, which captures the relationship between CHELSA temperature and PET. Its architecture handles varying spatial and temporal input sizes, enabling transferability across regions with different grid resolutions and across periods with different temporal window lengths. The model is trained for 400 epochs using ReLU activation, an Adam optimiser, and checkpointing to retain the best epoch. Training first uses only the selected sensor locations under data-sparse conditions, after which the best epoch is applied to the full spatial domain using gridded satellite inputs. This two-stage setup enables accurate large-scale PET estimation while reducing dependence on dense ground-based observations.

This method is evaluated against a state-of-the-art upscaling approach that aggregates high-resolution fields using km-scale spatial windows, as described by Wang et al. [23]. In this approach, average pooling is applied to reduce the spatial resolution and accelerate training, and the resulting surrogate model is subsequently deployed on the full-scale grid for large-area PET prediction.

Selecting an effective pixel-location method depends on how well each approach reduces the KS, W², and MPD discrepancies relative to the full domain. As shown in Figure 4, the 3DCNN accuracy under data scarcity highlights a clear difference between methods: the RL agent reaches its optimum using only 2% of the pixels, whereas the XGBoost-based approach requires 13%. RL performs better because it preserves the true spatial distribution, providing the surrogate hydrological model with inputs that remain consistent with the full spatial field and allowing the convolutional layers to learn PET dynamics from realistic patterns. XGBoost, by selecting pixels solely through feature importance, produces an irregular spatial pattern that no longer reflects the real distribution and introduces bias into the surrogate model. The loss curves show that the RL-selected dataset converges faster and reaches much lower validation loss than the XGBoost subset, demonstrating the importance of maintaining the true spatial structure when learning PET under data scarcity.

blocks.html: Figure 5 explain how the RL framework mitigates XGBoost-induced biases when applied to SRTM-derived DEM data for selecting suitable pixel locations. From the initial 13% of pixels identified by XGBoost, the RL agent evaluates percentile differences across the full domain to separate aligned from misaligned locations. This refinement improves representativeness using ±10 m and ±50 m accuracy thresholds. By integrating a genetic algorithm to optimise locations in sensitive regions, the RL procedure substantially reduces misalignment: under the ±10 m threshold, misaligned pixels fall from 429 to 259, with a similar reduction under the ±50 m threshold. Figure 5 further shows that the RL model can markedly reduce pixel coverage while preserving the spatial structure required for tasks such as in-situ hydrological sensor placement. This reduction also enhances surrogate model accuracy. Even with far fewer pixels (235 instead of 943), the RL framework maintains low MPD and alignment with regional terrain characteristics. Overall, the method identifies key sensor locations, reduces spatial misalignment by more than 70%, and provides a robust strategy for hydrological monitoring.

blocks.html: Large-scale model evaluation shows that integrating RL greatly improves the transferability of the 3DCNN, enabling accurate daily PET prediction across broad spatial domains. Relative to XGBoost, the RL-guided 3DCNN reduces RMSE by more than 50% and increases R² from 0.87 to 0.97. This gain reflects differences in model behaviour: XGBoost develops local, pixel-level biases due to the overfitting, whereas the 3DCNN_RL learns smoother, spatially coherent gradients (Figure 6). With pixel optimisation, the 3DCNN_RLOpt maintains strong predictive skill despite a much smaller input set, while XGBoost remains prone to spatial artefacts arising from pixel-independent decisions and patch boundaries. The RL-enhanced 3DCNN produces PET fields that are more consistent and physically plausible than those generated by XGBoost. When compared with the baseline upscaling approach, using a 5 km spatial scale, the proposed RL-based surrogate model shows clear gains: the 3DCNN_RL improves R<sup>2</sup> by 18%, while the 3DCNN_RLOpt variant yields a 13% increase.

blocks.html: Reliable large-scale daily PET estimation needs well-placed in-situ sensors and models that fuse their observations with satellite-derived products. This study proposes a reinforcement learning-based framework that optimises monitoring locations by identifying representative pixels in gridded DEM data, such as SRTM. Compared with XGBoost, the RL approach reduces misaligned pixels by more than 70%, retaining only the most informative locations while preserving the underlying spatial structure. Coupled with a 3DCNN surrogate model, the framework lowers training costs by relying on a sparse yet representative subset that captures essential spatial patterns and remains transferable across the full domain. Using 2% of the spatial data locations, the method increases the model’s R² from 0.87 to 0.97 while maintaining spatially coherent and physically consistent PET fields. RL-guided pixel selection combined with surrogate modelling therefore offers a scalable and data-efficient alternative to computationally intensive physical models for PET estimation across heterogeneous landscapes.

Future work will extend this framework to calibrate multiple hydrological satellite products and to guide efficient sensor distribution, ensuring that strategically placed sensors provide useful in-situ data that can be integrated by surrogate modelling for large-scale prediction.
